extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists and short-story writers), early-career to experienced
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on how to judge which creative-writing ideas to pursue, which to shelve, and how to manage multiple ideas over time; aimed at fiction authors deciding what to write and when. Covers practical heuristics, mental checklists, idea-sourcing, and habits that improve idea-selection and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: “I don’t pursue a story unless I know how it ends.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having an ending prevents quitting and gives you a finite destination; the ending is the 'taste left in your mouth' and will make readers (and you) retroactively reassess the whole book. If you struggle to finish, ensure you at least have an ending or clear mile markers to aim for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion and excitement as primary selector
rubrics_metrics.description: “What are you most excited about?” — choose projects that spark passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write what you are emotionally invested in rather than chasing perceived market trends. Passion leads to better execution; note the caveat that when under contract you may need the separate skill of forcing yourself to write something you committed to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interact with and explore ideas (try writing them)
rubrics_metrics.description: “You have to meet a lot of your ideas and interact with them. You have to explore them. You have to try to write them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only through playing with and writing an idea do you learn its shape — whether it's a three-book idea, a plot twist, or something else. Exploration develops the instinct for an idea's potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep multiple ideas simmering (burner-stove model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Victoria’s 'six burner stove' metaphor: several ideas simmering, one on high heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow ideas long cook times (months to years); keep several projects in low-heat development so you can turn up the one that’s ready. This prevents premature commitment and lets ideas mature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the kitchen-sink approach (don't put every idea in one book)
rubrics_metrics.description: “You do not need to take every idea that excites you and put it into one book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find ‘flavors that work together’ and withhold ingredients that don’t belong; some ideas are better saved for separate works rather than forcing them into the same project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track ideas — write them down
rubrics_metrics.description: “I keep track of them. I write them down. You don’t write it down, it’s lost forever and you don’t get to use it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a notebook or journal (e.g., keep a pad by your bed) so spontaneous ideas and dream-ideas aren't lost. Periodically review collected ideas for usable seeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution matters more than the raw idea
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ideas are cheap… it's execution upon those ideas which is what really matters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compelling idea poorly executed won't succeed; what makes a book stand out is the author's ability to stretch and realize the idea across a whole work. Example: a clever moment rendered badly vs well-executed narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish books; learn to finish
rubrics_metrics.description: “Force yourself to finish books. Finishing teaches you how to write.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for early-career writers, completing projects is a primary training ground. Even imperfect finished books teach craft and how to evaluate ideas going forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shiny-new-idea syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Shiny new idea syndrome: dropping current work for a new, alluring idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This impulse leads to chronic abandonment and prevents learning to finish; recognize it as a cognitive trick and favor finishing unless there’s a compelling, diagnosed reason to switch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose why you're struggling before abandoning
rubrics_metrics.description: “You need to understand why you’re struggling. There’s a difference between struggling because you’re afraid… and struggling because you’re bored.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether struggle stems from fear of doing it justice, boredom, or external/personal factors. Different causes require different remedies (motivation strategies, changing a scene, addressing personal needs), not immediate abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have mile markers and create standout scenes/chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: “Have the ending, or at least points that you are excited about writing… Try to make this chapter or this scene someone’s favorite in the whole book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes or chapters you’re eager to write as waypoints to carry you through the middle; rework chapters to be showpieces that sustain interest and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a checklist to determine scope of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Howard’s checklist: is this an overarching story problem? a scene problem? a chapter problem? a 'me' problem (sick, hungry, meds, etc.)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before deciding to abandon, systematically rule out scene/chapter fixes and personal issues. Only after addressing those should abandonment be considered; the checklist helps avoid premature shelfing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your skill set and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of what your skills can accomplish and what they can’t; practice quick execution under constraints (TypeCast example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing strengths and limits helps you choose ideas you can execute well and identify when an idea requires skills you lack. Quick, time-limited exercises can reveal whether an idea is viable for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test ideas quickly by fleshing them out
rubrics_metrics.description: “You have an idea, you don’t need to spend a novel fleshing it out. See how quickly you can flesh it out to determine what it leads to.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do short experiments or rapid sketches to discover the idea’s trajectory; this is a low-cost way to evaluate potential before major investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose projects aligned with your goals
rubrics_metrics.description: “Take a look at what your goals are for that [project]… if you’re early career, the purpose of that book is not to sell — it’s to teach you how to write your second book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a project’s purpose is training, portfolio-building, commercial success, or personal fulfillment, and let that purpose guide whether to continue, revise, or shelve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh revision cost versus writing a new book
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandon or shelve when revising a book to desired quality would be as much work as writing a new book without guaranteed success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pragmatic cost/benefit comparison can justify shelving a project; shelved projects can free resources for a new, better book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow ideas to steep long-term
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ideas 'steep' for six months to three or four years before being pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patience often improves an idea’s viability and your readiness to write it; long-term incubation reduces premature trunking and increases the chance of completing the project once started.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find passion within constraints — adapt the core idea
rubrics_metrics.description: “Take the core of the idea and find something you are passionate about.” (Dan’s MTG example: turn the core into a heist story.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When external constraints or assignments limit scope, identify a sub-aspect or framing that genuinely excites you and build the project around that to preserve motivation and execution quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate idea sources (dream journal homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: Keep a dream journal for a week; write down everything upon waking and review for ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured habits for idea capture (dream journals, notebooks) supply raw material for projects and help you notice recurring themes worth exploring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t chase the market
rubrics_metrics.description: “Don’t chase the market! … There is not a market for any particular genre or style. What there’s a market for is stuff that’s awesome.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid picking projects solely because you think they’ll sell; instead, write the most awesome version of what excites you — that’s what readers respond to.
